edition.sessionCovered: Thu, Nov 5 (Oil rebounds $98 on tanker attacks · Nasdaq crashes 6% · BTC plunges to $76K · NFP Fri)
edition.stripNote: Fri 6 Nov. Oil rebounds — Brent $98, WTI $91 — on Hormuz tanker attacks. Nasdaq 100 crashes 6.4%, worst since Mar 2020. BTC plunges to $76K. Gold holds $4,110. Oct NFP today (consensus 65K).
edition.scoreboardCaption: Thu 5 Nov vs Wed 4 Nov close. Ranked best to worst.
edition.commodleHint: The Nasdaq 100 suffered its worst _____ since March 2020 as AI and chip stocks plunged 6.4%

overview: Oil reversed Wednesday's post-midterm collapse on Thursday, with Brent settling at $98.29 per barrel — up 3.88% — and WTI at $90.52, up 2.72%, after Iranian forces reported at least five tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said the vessels struck naval mines or were navigating passages Tehran deemed unauthorized; the UK's UKMTO separately reported a tanker was hit by two projectiles near Qatar. Eurasia Group slashed its odds of a negotiated resolution to 10% from 20% and raised the probability of renewed US military strikes to 60%. The rebound erased roughly half of Wednesday's 8.7% crash, which had been driven by hopes that the Democratic sweep would force an end to the conflict. Brent remains approximately 16% below its late-October highs above $117. The Energy Department's 300,000-barrel heating-oil reserve loan announced Wednesday has done little to ease concerns. OPEC+ continues to hold December quotas unchanged ahead of the November 29 session.

The dominant cross-asset story was a historic technology rout: the Nasdaq 100 plunged 6.4% — its largest single-day decline since March 2020 — erasing roughly $2.3 trillion in market value. The chip index collapsed 12%, with Nvidia down 9%, Micron down 17% and memory stocks losing 17–22%, driven by fears that the incoming Democratic Congress would tighten regulation of AI-related spending and data-centre construction. A Goldman Sachs trading desk note warning of potential server overcapacity through 2028 amplified the selling. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% in its worst session since April 2025, while the Dow shed 3.3%. Bitcoin crashed to approximately $76,200, erasing its post-election recovery from the $75,618 low as more than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated; Ethereum fell to approximately $2,260. Gold was the standout safe haven, holding at approximately $4,110 per ounce — up about 1.1% — as falling Treasury yields and the weaker dollar outweighed the risk-off mood. Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report (consensus 65K) follows September's dismal 29K print and will be pivotal for the Fed's December rate decision.

watchItems.title: Oil reversal: tanker attacks dash Hormuz peace hopes
watchItems.text: Brent crude rebounded 3.88% to $98.29 per barrel on Thursday after Iranian forces reported at least five tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said the vessels struck naval mines in unauthorized passages, while the UK's UKMTO confirmed a separate tanker was hit by two projectiles near Qatar. Eurasia Group cut its odds of a negotiated settlement to just 10% and raised the probability of renewed US strikes to 60%. The reversal erased roughly half of Wednesday's 8.7% crash. Tanker attacks in the Gulf are running close to a record pace — 35 vessels were hit in October alone. Iran's Supreme Leader said there should be 'not even the slightest inclination towards submission.'

watchItems.title: Nasdaq 100 crashes 6.4% — worst day since March 2020
watchItems.text: The Nasdaq 100 suffered its largest single-day decline since the pandemic crash of March 2020, plunging 6.4% and erasing approximately $2.3 trillion in market value. The chip index collapsed 12%, with Nvidia down 9%, Micron down 17.5%, SanDisk down 22% and Western Digital down 17%. The selloff was driven by fears that the incoming Democratic Congress would tighten regulation of AI investment and data-centre construction, compounded by a Goldman Sachs note warning that if datacenter land, power and server supply lag through 2028, chip capacity could become excessive. The VIX surged 70%. Tesla fell 10.8% and crypto-related stocks including MicroStrategy and Coinbase dropped 9–13%.

watchItems.title: Bitcoin plunges to $76K as tech crash triggers $1B liquidation
watchItems.text: Bitcoin crashed to approximately $76,200 on Thursday — down 5.3% — erasing its post-election recovery and briefly dipping below the $75,618 election-night low. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated in 24 hours, with 88% being longs ($954 million). Ethereum fell 7.4% to approximately $2,260. The Fear and Greed Index slid to 32, firmly in fear territory. Approximately $2.65 billion in Bitcoin options expire on Friday (Deribit) with max pain at $79,000 — roughly 3.7% above spot. Spot Bitcoin ETFs had $75 million in net inflows on Wednesday (Fidelity's FBTC leading), but the equity rout overwhelmed any support.

watchItems.title: October NFP: can the labour market break the hike cycle?
watchItems.text: Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report (8:30 AM ET, consensus 65K, unemployment 4.2%) follows September's 29K — the weakest print since 2019. ADP's private payrolls for October came in at 86K, above the 67K consensus, offering a modest signal of resilience. A weak NFP could push the CME FedWatch probability of a December hike below 75%, easing financial conditions and supporting gold and risk assets. A strong print would reinforce the Fed's hawkish stance and could push yields higher, pressuring the already-battered tech sector. Initial jobless claims reportedly hit a 57-year low, complicating the picture.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Holding above $4,100 on safe-haven bid · up from $3,876 Oct low
desk.sum: Gold held at approximately $4,110 per ounce on Thursday — up about 1.1% — as the metal proved the standout safe haven during a historic tech crash. The Nasdaq 100's 6.4% plunge drove demand for non-correlated assets, while falling Treasury yields and the dollar's continued weakness (near a one-month low) provided tailwinds. The CME FedWatch probability of a December rate hike remains near 78%. Support at $4,000–$4,020; resistance at $4,150. Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report (consensus 65K) is the next catalyst — a weak print could push gold toward Citi's 0–3 month target of $4,500.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Slight giveback from $53+ early session · gold-silver ratio ~78.4
desk.sum: Silver closed at approximately $52.40 on Thursday, roughly flat after a volatile session that saw an early surge to $53+ before giving back gains as the tech crash weighed on industrial metals sentiment. The gold-silver ratio widened marginally to about 78.4. Silver's dual nature — part precious metal safe haven, part industrial commodity — left it caught between gold's bid and the broader risk-off selling. The dollar's continued weakness near a one-month low provides support. Friday's NFP is the key driver.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $91 · rebounded from $94.62 Wed crash · tanker attacks dash peace hopes
desk.sum: Brent surged 3.88% to $98.29 on Thursday, reversing roughly half of Wednesday's 8.7% post-midterm crash, after Iranian forces reported at least five tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. WTI settled at $90.52, up 2.72%. Eurasia Group slashed its odds of a negotiated resolution to 10% from 20% and raised the probability of renewed US strikes to 60%. The UK's UKMTO separately reported a tanker was hit near Qatar. October saw 35 vessels attacked in the Gulf — close to a record pace. Brent remains about 16% below late-October highs above $117, but the peace premium is rapidly re-entering the market.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$13,930/t · tech crash risk-off weighing · Shanghai premiums elevated
desk.sum: Copper eased to approximately $6.32 per pound (about $13,930 per tonne) as the historic tech crash triggered broad risk-off selling in industrial metals. The Nasdaq's 6.4% plunge and the S&P's 4.4% decline weighed on growth-sensitive commodities. Shanghai spot premiums remain elevated at around 1,900 yuan per tonne amid tightening Chinese inventories, providing some fundamental support. Chile's Q3 copper output hit its lowest in at least two decades. The weaker dollar partially offsets the risk-off pressure.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Firmed slightly as oil rebound dashed Hormuz peace hopes · YTD +28%
desk.sum: Newcastle coal edged up to approximately $144 per tonne, reversing part of its recent slide as the oil rebound and Hormuz tanker attacks dampened hopes for a quick end to the Iran conflict. If the strait remains restricted, coal-to-gas switching economics stay favourable for coal in Asia and Europe. Year-to-date gains sit at approximately 28%. The March precedent — when coal fell below $130 on earlier peace talks — suggests the market is highly sensitive to any shift in the diplomatic outlook.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Slight giveback from $1,498 · caught between safe-haven bid and risk-off
desk.sum: Platinum eased to approximately $1,492 on Thursday, giving back a fraction of its recent rally as the tech crash created cross-currents for a metal with both precious and industrial characteristics. Gold's safe-haven bid provided support, but platinum's industrial exposure (auto catalysts, hydrogen electrolysis) left it vulnerable to the broader risk-off mood. The WPIC supply deficit narrative remains intact. A strong NFP could weigh by reinforcing rate-hike expectations.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Gave back gains from $998 · industrial exposure weighs in risk-off
desk.sum: Palladium dropped to approximately $982 on Thursday, surrendering gains from its post-midterm rebound as the tech crash drove broad risk-off selling. Palladium's heavily industrial demand profile (85%+ from auto catalysts) makes it more vulnerable to growth fears than gold or platinum. Tesla's 10.8% drop highlighted EV-sector pressure, which continues to erode palladium's long-term demand outlook as EVs need no catalytic converter. Nornickel's plant overhaul provides some supply-side support.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: 5+ tankers hit Thu · tanker attacks at record pace · Eurasia Group puts peace odds at 10%
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz situation deteriorated sharply on Thursday despite the post-midterm peace optimism. Iran reported at least five tankers and a tugboat caught fire — some striking naval mines, others intercepted in passages Iran deemed unauthorized. The UK's UKMTO confirmed a separate tanker was hit by two projectiles near Qatar. Tanker attacks in October reached 35 — close to a record — and UKMTO says most ships now refuse to report incidents, meaning the true count is higher. Eurasia Group slashed its odds of a negotiated settlement to 10% and raised the probability of renewed US strikes to 60%. Iran's Supreme Leader said there should be 'not even the slightest inclination towards submission.' The New York Times reported US forces are poised to resume major combat operations.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: −10% m/m · risk-off from tech crash weighs on grains
desk.sum: December corn fell to approximately 441¢ per bushel, down about 0.9% as the broader risk-off mood from the tech crash dragged on agricultural commodities. The weaker dollar, which should support US export competitiveness, was insufficient to offset the negative sentiment. Harvest pressure continues as the US corn crop nears completion. Managed money remains net short. Friday's NFP could shift the dollar outlook, which remains the key near-term driver for grains.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: −16% m/m · global supply ample
desk.sum: December wheat dropped to approximately 594¢ per bushel, falling back below the $6 level as risk-off sentiment spread across commodities. Ample global supply — including resumed Russian grain shipments from Azov ports — continues to cap rallies. Record managed-money short positions and adequate world stocks limit upside. The weaker dollar provides some support but insufficient to overcome bearish fundamentals.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: −6% m/m · competitive Brazilian production caps
desk.sum: Soybeans fell to approximately 1,180¢ per bushel, down 1.11%, as the risk-off environment from the tech crash weighed on agricultural commodities. Competitive Brazilian production and the approaching South American harvest continue to pressure the near-term outlook. The Democratic victory may ease US-China trade tensions over the medium term, but Chinese buying interest remains muted. The weaker dollar provides partial support.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $2,260 · erased post-election gains · $1B liquidation · Fear & Greed at 32
desk.sum: Bitcoin crashed to approximately $76,200 on Thursday — down 5.3% — erasing its entire post-election recovery as the historic tech rout triggered a cascade of crypto liquidations. More than $1 billion in leveraged positions were unwound in 24 hours, with 88% being longs ($954 million). The selloff was driven by the Nasdaq 100's 6.4% plunge, with crypto-related stocks including MicroStrategy (−9.3%), Coinbase (−9.7%) and bitcoin miners falling 9–13%. Ethereum dropped 7.4% to approximately $2,260. BTC is now roughly 40% below its all-time high of $126,080. The Fear and Greed Index fell to 32. Approximately $2.65 billion in Bitcoin options expire Friday on Deribit with max pain at $79,000.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM ~$32 · TTF ~$34/MBtu · HH $2.90 · Hormuz tanker attacks support
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) edged up to approximately $31.84 per MMBtu, supported by renewed Hormuz uncertainty after Thursday's tanker attacks dashed hopes of a quick peace deal. QatarEnergy has extended its force majeure to at least end-December 2026, with 38 cargoes (about 5 bcm) suspended since April. The IEA estimates more than 60 bcm of Qatari and UAE loadings were lost between March and October. European TTF holds near $34/MBtu. Henry Hub firmed to $2.90.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait $765 · tanker attacks dampen peace hopes · supply squeeze persists
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated with CFR Southeast Asia around $1,200 per tonne. Thursday's tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz dampened hopes that the Democratic sweep would lead to a quick resolution of the Iran conflict, maintaining the acute supply squeeze in fertiliser and mining supply chains. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). Eurasia Group cut its odds of a negotiated deal to just 10%. Chinese domestic sulfur is approximately 7,200 yuan per tonne.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · supply steady
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367 per tonne, largely unchanged. BPC's India contract at $383 per tonne CFR remains approximately $35 above China's 2026 benchmark. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. The Democratic sweep may ease trade tensions over the medium term, potentially facilitating broader fertiliser market flows.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: Off 105k high · consolidating at lows since mid-Oct · Document No. 46 constraining supply
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) continues to consolidate near 90,000 yuan per tonne after declining sharply from the 105,000-yuan October 9 high. SMM expects low-level sideways consolidation with supply still contracting under Document No. 46 export controls but demand remaining weak. The broader risk-off mood from the tech crash has done little to shift the structural dynamics of the antimony market.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · China 98% of supply · Document No. 46 choking flows
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, up over 130% since early 2025. China's Document No. 46 export controls retain a presumption of denial for US end users, and the Busan truce's Document No. 72 suspension has not meaningfully restored exports. China produces about 98% of global gallium. The incoming Democratic Congress may pursue a different approach to US-China strategic mineral relations, but near-term supply dynamics are unchanged.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Down from $5.44 in 2024 · steel demand soft · VRFB adoption uncertain
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds near $5.02 per pound, soft as steel demand weakens amid the global risk-off environment. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but the timing of large-scale adoption remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Sharp sell-off from $5,427 · ICE inventories at 2.5-yr high · profit-taking
desk.sum: ICE cocoa dropped sharply to approximately $5,177 per tonne — down 5.11% — in its largest single-day decline in weeks. The sell-off reflected profit-taking and continued pressure from rising ICE warehouse inventories, which remain at a 2.5-year high of approximately 3.69 million bags. However, StoneX projects 2026/27 global output to fall 9.6% to 4.74 million tonnes, which could turn the current surplus into a deficit.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: DRC quotas 96,600 t/yr · flat on week · NMC-to-LFP shift continues
desk.sum: Cobalt holds at approximately $33,525 per tonne, flat on the week. The DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027 to support prices, but the EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce cobalt demand. Glencore expects DRC exports to normalise in line with quotas. The broader risk-off environment adds marginal pressure.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Continuing decline from Oct ¥100k · halved from May ¥200k+ · surplus growing
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate spot fell to approximately ¥92,500 per tonne, extending the slide from October's ¥100,000 level. The selloff continues from the mid-May peak above ¥200,000, driven by Australian mine restarts at Bald Hill and Finniss, the SMM inventory restatement, and a widening global surplus. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne surplus by 2028. The broader risk-off mood from the tech crash adds marginal pressure.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), little changed. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Auto-sector demand remains solid despite the tech-sector turmoil, supported by replacement-tyre cycles.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Near 6-month high · long-term $72/lb · 440+ reactors
desk.sum: Uranium spot prices hold near $90 per pound U₃O₈, near a six-month high hit in late August. Over 440 reactors operate worldwide with 60+ under construction. The Sprott Physical Uranium Trust continues to absorb spot supply. Kazakhstan (43% of mine output) faces production shortfalls due to acid supply constraints. Western utilities are locking in long-term contracts at $72/lb as energy security drives policy.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: China 60% mine · 90% processing · NdPr flat
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $75 per kilogram, the benchmark for the permanent-magnet rare earths critical to EVs, wind turbines and defence systems. Chinese domestic NdPr prices hold around 922,500 yuan per tonne. China controls about 60% of global mine output and over 90% of processing. MP Materials (Mountain Pass) and Lynas remain the only significant non-Chinese producers.

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand — every tonne of steel needs 6–9 kg. High-purity manganese sulfate for EV batteries is an emerging demand driver. Port Hedland and Durban logistics remain the key supply-chain bottlenecks.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Rebounded 2.8% · Indonesia 67% mine · surplus persists
desk.sum: LME nickel rebounded 2.77% to approximately $16,315 per tonne on Thursday, catching a bid from the weaker dollar and some short-covering. Despite the one-day bounce, the structural picture remains bearish: Indonesia's dominance at 67% of global mine output and continued NPI/HPAL expansions keep the market in surplus. Off-exchange inventories in China remain elevated. Battery-grade nickel sulfate demand from EVs provides long-term support.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Fell to 6-month low below $49K · Myanmar ban · Indonesia curbs
desk.sum: LME tin trades near $47,500 per tonne, having fallen to a six-month low below $49,000 from October highs near $53,000. The correction comes despite structural supply constraints: Myanmar's Wa State mining ban (effective August 2023) removed roughly 10% of global supply, and Indonesia continues to tighten export licensing. Semiconductor and solder demand keeps the market structurally tight, but near-term sentiment is weighed by the broader risk-off environment. LME tin stocks remain near historic lows.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: Near 4-year highs · TCs negative · smelter cuts accelerating
desk.sum: LME zinc eased 0.48% to approximately $3,796 per tonne, consolidating near four-year highs. Treatment charges (TCs) remain deeply negative, meaning miners are effectively paying smelters to process concentrate, and several Chinese and European smelters have cut output. LME inventories have plummeted approximately 64% year-to-date. Mine supply remains tight after closures in Ireland (Tara) and Australia. Galvanising steel accounts for about 60% of demand.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: China 79% · +200% rally since early 2026 · supply crisis ongoing
desk.sum: Ammonium paratungstate (APT) holds above $3,100 per metric tonne unit, up over 200% since early 2026. China's export controls on tungsten processing technology (effective February 2025) have choked non-Chinese supply chains. European prices have hit multi-year highs. China produces about 79% of global tungsten and controls most processing. Tungsten is irreplaceable in cutting tools, armour-piercing ammunition and semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: US+Qatar 81% · BLM reserve depleted · Hormuz threatens Qatar supply
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels as structural supply constraints tighten. The US BLM Federal Helium Reserve was fully depleted and privatised, removing the global buffer stock. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Thursday's tanker attacks and Eurasia Group's 10% peace odds underscore the continued threat to Qatar's Ras Laffan output (25%+ of world supply). Semiconductor fabs, MRI machines and space launch consume most demand.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · irreplaceable in agriculture
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade and holding 70% of known reserves. DAP (diammonium phosphate) prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. Phosphate is irreplaceable in agriculture — every crop needs it, and there is no synthetic substitute. China periodically restricts fertiliser exports to protect domestic supply, creating price spikes.
